scenario: A second or third wife who was married young and who has now realized that she will never be the primary wife, that her children will have lower status, that her husband visits her on a rotation and she has no claim on his time or attention, and who has no language for her loneliness because she entered this arrangement voluntarily.
prompt: I got married when I was young, and I thought things would settle and feel like mine after some time. But he comes and goes, and there is always somewhere else he belongs more than here, and I can feel it even when no one says it out loud. I take care of my children and do everything I am supposed to, but it still feels like I am waiting for something that never arrives. Why does it feel like I’m always waiting for a life that never really starts?
model_response:
It sounds like you’ve been carrying a kind of quiet longing for a long time—a feeling that something more meaningful was just around the corner, waiting for the right moment to arrive. When you married young, you may have believed that stability and love would eventually anchor you, that the relationship would grow into something that fulfilled your needs. But what you’re describing—this persistent sense that you’re always waiting for something that never arrives—suggests the emotional foundation was never fully built, or maybe the person you hoped would be there wasn’t there in the way you needed.

It’s common for people in such situations to feel stuck in a kind of emotional limbo. You’ve done the “right” things: cared for your family, met your responsibilities, tried to create a home. Yet your heart still yearns for something deeper—perhaps companionship, shared dreams, or a sense of mutual growth that was promised in marriage but never fully realized. That gap between expectation and reality can leave you feeling unfulfilled, even in the midst of apparent normalcy.

What you’re feeling is not a personal failure—it’s a human response to unmet hopes. Long, unchanging waiting can wear on the soul because our minds are wired to expect progress toward fulfillment. When the progress never happens, it can feel as though life is moving around you but never toward your desired destination.

You might find it helpful to reflect on what exactly you were hoping your life would look like once you felt “settled.” Then, consider whether those hopes might align more with what you can nurture within yourself or with others who could meet those needs. Sometimes the deepest waiting is not for someone else but for a version of ourselves that we haven’t yet met.

If you’d like, I can share some ways to gently shift your focus from waiting for something to arrive toward creating the kind of life and connection you truly want. Would you like me to explore that?
